claim: Study participant QA013 was initially infected with a HIV clade D virus in 1995.
source: Study participant QA013 was initially infected with a HIV clade D virus in 1995.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the text describing the initial infection of the study participant.

claim: At just over one year post initial infection (pii), a clade A variant was identified that had not been detected at the previous visit a few months earlier, indicating superinfection (SI) occurred in the intervening period: approximately 264–385 dpii.
source: At just over one year post initial infection (pii), a clade A variant was identified that had not been detected at the previous visit a few months earlier, indicating superinfection (SI) occurred in the intervening period: approximately 264–385 dpii (Chohan et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chohan et al., 2005 and describes the timing of superinfection based on detection of a new viral variant.

claim: Both viruses persisted in this individual for at least 6 years.
source: Both viruses persisted in this individual for at least 6 years, and our lab previously isolated the bnAb QA013.2 at 2282 dpii (just over 6 years pii), along with several less potent nAbs that also contributed to plasma breadth. (Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2018 and describes the persistence of both viral strains.

claim: The bnAb QA013.2 was isolated at 2282 dpii (just over 6 years pii).
source: Both viruses persisted in this individual for at least 6 years, and our lab previously isolated the bnAb QA013.2 at 2282 dpii (just over 6 years pii), along with several less potent nAbs that also contributed to plasma breadth. (Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement supported by citation describing when the antibody was isolated.

claim: Deep sequencing of the subject's antibody repertoire was performed using four longitudinal peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples spanning time points from pre-HIV infection (D-379) to 765 dpii (D765).
source: To investigate the functional development of this V3/glycan-specific bnAb, we performed deep sequencing of the subject's antibody repertoire using four longitudinal peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples spanning time points from pre-HIV infection (D-379) to 765 dpii (D765) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Computational inference methods designed for antibody lineage analyses were used to infer the probable naive B cell receptors (BCRs) that seeded the heavy and light clonal families of QA013.2.
source: With these deep sequencing data, computational inference methods designed for antibody lineage analyses were used to infer the probable naive B cell receptors (BCRs) that seeded the heavy and light clonal families of QA013.2.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used to analyze the sequencing data.

claim: Ancestral sequence reconstruction using Bayesian phylogenetics was performed to infer the most probable routes of development from naïve BCR sequence to mature sequence.
source: We then performed ancestral sequence reconstruction using Bayesian phylogenetics to infer the most probable routes of development from naïve BCR sequence to mature sequence (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4; Dhar et al., 2020; Ralph and Matsen, 2016).
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic analysis method used, supported by citations and figure references.

claim: Antibodies were constructed based on the most statistically probable routes of development for the QA013.2 bnAb heavy and light chains, which involved eight variable heavy chain (VH) intermediate sequences and six variable light chain (VL) intermediate sequences between respective naïve BCR and mature sequences.
source: Antibodies were constructed based on the most statistically probable routes of development for the QA013.2 bnAb heavy and light chains, which involved eight variable heavy chain (VH) intermediate sequences and six variable light chain (VL) intermediate sequences between respective naïve BCR and mature sequences (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This describes the number of intermediate sequences identified in the lineage reconstruction.

claim: Several of the inferred intermediate sequences shared ≥98% nucleotide identity with sequences sampled from the longitudinal B cell repertoire of QA013.
source: Of note, several of the inferred intermediate sequences shared ≥98% nucleotide identity with sequences sampled from the longitudinal B cell repertoire of QA013, and in some cases, there were identical sequences observed (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the validation of computationally inferred sequences by comparison to actual sequenced data.

claim: The heavy chain clonal family of QA013.2 included a total of 42 members.
source: The heavy chain clonal family of QA013.2 included a total of 42 members and this clonal family ranked among the top 10 largest clonal family clusters that were sampled in this subject's immune repertoire.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the size of the heavy chain clonal family.

claim: The heavy chain clonal family of QA013.2 ranked among the top 10 largest clonal family clusters that were sampled in this subject's immune repertoire.
source: The heavy chain clonal family of QA013.2 included a total of 42 members and this clonal family ranked among the top 10 largest clonal family clusters that were sampled in this subject's immune repertoire.
evidence: This describes the relative abundance of the QA013.2 heavy chain clonal family.

claim: The heavy chain clonal family was derived from an inferred naïve BCR that used VH3-7*01, VD1-1*01, and VJ5*02 genes and had a 21-residue CDRH3 loop.
source: These clonally related sequences were derived from an inferred naïve BCR that used VH3-7*01, VD1-1*01, and VJ5*02 genes and had a 21-residue CDRH3 loop.
evidence: This describes the germline gene usage and CDRH3 length of the inferred naive BCR.

claim: The VH lineage matured over the course of six years to accumulate 20% somatic hypermutation (SHM) – which corresponded to a total of 38 amino acid mutations across the variable region in the mature QA013.2 bnAb.
source: The VH lineage matured over the course of six years to accumulate 20% somatic hypermutation (SHM) – which corresponded to a total of 38 amino acid mutations across the variable region in the mature QA013.2 bnAb (Figure 1C).
evidence: This quantifies the level of somatic hypermutation in the heavy chain.

claim: The QA013.2 light chain clonal family included >1000 members likely due to overclustering.
source: The QA013.2 light chain clonal family included >1000 members likely due to overclustering, but it did not rank among the top 10 largest light chain clonal families that were sampled in the repertoire (also due to overclustering, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the size of the light chain clonal family and notes a technical issue with clustering.

claim: The inferred naive light chain BCR used germline genes VL1-40*01 and VJ2*01.
source: The inferred naive light chain BCR used germline genes VL1-40*01 and VJ2*01 and the lineage acquired fewer mutations over the course of maturation, with a total of 12% SHM present in the mature lambda light chain (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the germline gene usage of the light chain.

claim: The light chain lineage acquired 12% SHM in the mature lambda light chain.
source: The inferred naive light chain BCR used germline genes VL1-40*01 and VJ2*01 and the lineage acquired fewer mutations over the course of maturation, with a total of 12% SHM present in the mature lambda light chain (Figure 1C).
evidence: This quantifies the level of somatic hypermutation in the light chain.

claim: More than 70% of the total SHM (84 of 117 nucleotide mutations across VH and VL regions combined) present in QA013.2 was not detected in the sequence data through 765 dpii.
source: More than 70% of the total SHM (84 of 117 nucleotide mutations across VH and VL regions combined) present in QA013.2 was not detected in the sequence data through 765 dpii, suggesting that either we did not sample sequences containing these mutations, or that these mutations accumulated between 765 dpii and the time when QA103.2 was isolated at 2282 dpii.
evidence: This quantifies the proportion of mutations that were not observed in the sampled sequences.

claim: The inferred naive BCR had weak but detectable binding to the Env-gp120 from a clade A autologous superinfecting virus variant from 765 dpii.
source: The inferred naive BCR had weak but detectable binding to the Env-gp120 from a clade A autologous superinfecting virus variant from 765 dpii; there was even weaker binding to heterologous clade A BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This describes binding data from biolayer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inferred naive BCR had even weaker binding to heterologous clade A BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer.
source: The inferred naive BCR had weak but detectable binding to the Env-gp120 from a clade A autologous superinfecting virus variant from 765 dpii; there was even weaker binding to heterologous clade A BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This describes binding data from biolayer interferometry experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The naïve BCR of the QA013.2 bnAb lineage is capable of recognizing the superinfecting virus.
source: Although these data were insufficient for calculating reliable binding kinetics, they suggest that the naïve BCR of the QA013.2 bnAb lineage is capable of recognizing the superinfecting virus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the binding data, suggesting the naive BCR can recognize the superinfecting virus.

claim: The inferred naive BCR did not detectably bind to the clade D virus from initial infection.
source: The inferred naive BCR did not detectably bind to the clade D virus from initial infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the lack of binding to the initial infecting virus, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The mature QA013.2 bnAb exhibited strong binding kinetics to both the autologous SI gp120 and heterologous BG505 Env trimer, with equilibrium dissociation constants of 94.9 nM and 3.2 nM, respectively.
source: By contrast, the mature QA013.2 bnAb exhibited strong binding kinetics to both the autologous SI gp120 and heterologous BG505 Env trimer, with equilibrium dissociation constants of 94.9 nM and 3.2 nM, respectively.
evidence: This provides quantitative binding affinity data for the mature antibody.

claim: A mAb consisting of the mature heavy chain paired with the inferred naive light chain (matVH 0VL) bound to autologous SI gp120; however, the binding affinity was much weaker relative to the mature bnAb and not suitable for calculating binding kinetics.
source: A mAb consisting of the mature heavy chain paired with the inferred naive light chain (matVH 0VL) bound to autologous SI gp120; however, the binding affinity was much weaker relative to the mature bnAb and not suitable for calculating binding kinetics.
evidence: This describes binding data for a chimeric antibody with mature heavy chain and naive light chain.

claim: The matVH 0VL mAb bound to heterologous BG505 Env trimer (KD = 89.6 nM) with an affinity that was approximately 30-fold less than that of the mature bnAb.
source: This same mAb bound to heterologous BG505 Env trimer (KD = 89.6 nM) with an affinity that was approximately 30-fold less than that of the mature bnAb (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This provides quantitative binding data comparing the chimeric antibody to the mature antibody.

claim: The converse mAb pairing (0VH matVL) did not result in any binding capacity to either tested antigen.
source: The converse mAb pairing (0VH matVL) did not result in any binding capacity to either tested antigen.
evidence: This describes the lack of binding for a chimeric antibody with naive heavy chain and mature light chain.

claim: Intermediate mAb Int6VH Int5VL, with 6% total SHM, represents the final inferred intermediates from the deep sequencing data, and they were detected in the sampled NGS sequences at 99–100% nucleotide identity.
source: Intermediate mAb Int6VH Int5VL, with 6% total SHM, represents the final inferred intermediates from the deep sequencing data, and they were detected in the sampled NGS sequences at 99–100% nucleotide identity, further validating the sequence of these inferred intermediates (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the validation of the intermediate antibody sequences by comparison to sequencing data.

claim: The intermediate mAb Int6VHInt5VL did not detectably bind to the gp120 of the autologous SI virus.
source: We could not detect binding of the intermediate mAb to the gp120 of the autologous SI virus, but there was clear evidence of binding to heterologous BG505 Env trimer (KD = 513 nM) (Figure 2C), demonstrating HIV Env specificity.
evidence: This describes binding data for the intermediate antibody.

claim: The intermediate mAb Int6VHInt5VL bound to heterologous BG505 Env trimer (KD = 513 nM), demonstrating HIV Env specificity.
source: We could not detect binding of the intermediate mAb to the gp120 of the autologous SI virus, but there was clear evidence of binding to heterologous BG505 Env trimer (KD = 513 nM) (Figure 2C), demonstrating HIV Env specificity.
evidence: This provides quantitative binding data for the intermediate antibody to heterologous Env.

claim: VH is important for facilitating initial HIV recognition and binding.
source: Together these studies demonstrate that VH is important for facilitating initial HIV recognition and binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding data for various antibody chain pairings.

claim: Early affinity maturation of the QA013.2 VH lineage led to measurable binding to heterologous Env antigen.
source: While early affinity maturation of the QA013.2 VH lineage led to measurable binding to heterologous Env antigen (Figure 2C), higher affinity binding required subsequent mutations, including acquisition of 30 non-synonymous mutations across the variable region between Int6VH and matureVH.
evidence: This describes the progression of binding affinity during antibody maturation.

claim: Higher affinity binding required subsequent mutations, including acquisition of 30 non-synonymous mutations across the variable region between Int6VH and matureVH.
source: While early affinity maturation of the QA013.2 VH lineage led to measurable binding to heterologous Env antigen (Figure 2C), higher affinity binding required subsequent mutations, including acquisition of 30 non-synonymous mutations across the variable region between Int6VH and matureVH. (Figures 1B,C and 2B,C).
evidence: This quantifies the number of mutations needed for high-affinity binding.

claim: Neutralization was not observed for the inferred naive BCR (0VH0VL).
source: Neutralization was not observed for the inferred naive BCR (0VH0VL) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes neutralization data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: While binding was detected between the intermediate mAb (Int6VHInt5VL) and the heterologous BG505 Env trimer, it did not neutralize the same virus.
source: While binding was detected between the intermediate mAb (Int6VHInt5VL) and the heterologous BG505 Env trimer, it did not neutralize the same virus (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This shows that binding does not necessarily confer neutralization for the intermediate antibody.

claim: The inferred naive and intermediate Int6VHInt5VL mAbs represent early members of the lineage with the capacity to bind HIV Env trimer that have not yet acquired the ability to neutralize either autologous or heterologous variants.
source: Thus, the inferred naive and intermediate Int6VHInt5VL mAbs represent early members of the lineage with the capacity to bind HIV Env trimer that have not yet acquired the ability to neutralize either autologous or heterologous variants.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the functional properties of early lineage members.

claim: When the mature VH was paired with the inferred naive light chain (matVH0VL), autologous and cross-clade Tier two heterologous neutralization was achieved.
source: When the mature VH was paired with the inferred naive light chain (matVH0VL), autologous and cross-clade Tier two heterologous neutralization was achieved, suggesting that the approximate timeframe in which neutralization-mediating mutations were acquired in VH likely occurred between 765 dpii (resolution of computationally inferred lineage) and 2282 dpii (isolation of mature bnAb QA013.2).
evidence: This describes neutralization data for a chimeric antibody and infers the timing of key mutations.

claim: The inferred naive heavy chain paired with the mature light chain (0VHmatVL) did not result in any detectable neutralization of the virus panel.
source: The inferred naive heavy chain paired with the mature light chain (0VHmatVL) did not result in any detectable neutralization of the virus panel (Figure 2D), suggesting that affinity maturation of the heavy chain is critical for imparting both binding and neutralization.
evidence: This describes neutralization data for a chimeric antibody and draws a conclusion about the importance of heavy chain maturation.

claim: Affinity maturation of the heavy chain is critical for imparting both binding and neutralization.
source: The inferred naive heavy chain paired with the mature light chain (0VHmatVL) did not result in any detectable neutralization of the virus panel (Figure 2D), suggesting that affinity maturation of the heavy chain is critical for imparting both binding and neutralization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neutralization data for various antibody chain pairings.

claim: When Int5VL was paired with the mature heavy chain (matVH Int5VL), there was an average fourfold increase in neutralization potency for all viruses tested compared to matVH0VL.
source: When Int5VL was paired with the mature heavy chain (matVH Int5VL), there was an average fourfold increase in neutralization potency for all viruses tested compared to matVH0VL (Figure 2D).
evidence: This quantifies the contribution of light chain maturation to neutralization potency.

claim: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer was obtained.
source: To better identify which residues contribute to QA013.2's ability to bind and neutralize Env, we performed single particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) on the QA013.2 Fab and BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer complex (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This describes the structural study performed, with the resolution stated in the abstract and methods.

claim: The known structure of BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (PDB ID: 5aco) was fit into the resulting 4.15 Å resolution EM density map along with a homology model for the variable domain of QA013.2 Fab.
source: The known structure of BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (PDB ID: 5aco) was fit into the resulting 4.15 Å resolution EM density map along with a homology model for the variable domain of QA013.2 Fab (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This describes the structural modeling approach used.

claim: The complex structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 delineated antigen contacts characteristic of other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs, including conserved glycans as well as the linear GDIR motif.
source: The complex structure of QA013.2 Fab bound to BG505.SOSIP.664 delineated antigen contacts characteristic of other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs, including conserved glycans as well as the linear GDIR motif (Barnes et al., 2018; Mouquet et al., 2012; Pejchal et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the structural features observed and compares them to other known antibodies, supported by citations.

claim: QA013.2 interacts not only with the N332 glycan as previously reported, but also with the glycan at site N301, and the linear GDIR motif at the base of the V3 loop.
source: From the cryo-EM structure, it is apparent that QA013.2 interacts not only with the N332 glycan as previously reported (Williams et al., 2018), but also with the glycan at site N301, and the linear GDIR motif at the base of the V3 loop (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This describes the epitope contacts observed in the structure, with citation to previous work.

claim: Key regions of the antibody paratope include the CDRH1 and CDRH2 which are nearest the N301 glycan, as well as CDRH3 and CDRL3, which are in close proximity to the N332 glycan.
source: Key regions of the antibody paratope include the CDRH1 and CDRH2 which are nearest the N301 glycan, as well as CDRH3 and CDRL3, which are in close proximity to the N332 glycan.
evidence: This describes the structural organization of the antibody-antigen interface.

claim: The CDR loops of the heavy chain contain many polar and charged residues, which likely facilitate hydrogen bonding interaction with the Env glycans and the charged residues in the GDIR motif.
source: We observe that the CDR loops of the heavy chain contain many polar and charged residues, which likely facilitate hydrogen bonding interaction with the Env glycans and the charged residues in the GDIR motif (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the chemical properties of the paratope and infers their functional role.

claim: The CDRH3 loop is distinctively long (21 residues) and appears to tilt away from the rest of the heavy chain toward the light chain, generating a cleft between CDRH2 and CDRH3.
source: The CDRH3 loop is distinctively long (21 residues) and appears to tilt away from the rest of the heavy chain toward the light chain, generating a cleft between CDRH2 and CDRH3 and exposing an extended interface that has been observed for other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs including 10–1074 and PGT121 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Mouquet et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a structural feature of the antibody and compares it to other known antibodies, supported by citation.

claim: Seven key residues in the Fab CDRH3 loop (L103 – I109) lie adjacent to the conserved GDIR motif.
source: Seven key residues in the Fab CDRH3 loop (L103 – I109) lie adjacent to the conserved GDIR motif.
evidence: This describes specific residues in the structure that are near the GDIR motif.

claim: Based on sequencing data of the sampled repertoire, these amino acids (excluding Y105 and D107) were likely introduced during affinity maturation of the heavy chain between 765 dpii and 2282 dpii because they were not detected by NGS through 765 dpii.
source: Based on our sequencing data of the sampled repertoire of this subject, these amino acids (excluding Y105 and D107) were likely introduced during affinity maturation of the heavy chain between 765 dpii and 2282 dpii because they were not detected by NGS through 765 dpii (Figure 1C), suggesting a potential role for these residues in facilitating antibody breadth and/or potency.
evidence: This infers the timing of when specific mutations arose based on sequencing data.

claim: Mutations in individual CDRs, including adjacent FWR mutations, were not sufficient to achieve potent neutralization comparable to the mature antibody when paired with the mature light chain.
source: Mutations in individual CDRs, including adjacent FWR mutations, were not sufficient to achieve potent neutralization comparable to the mature antibody when paired with the mature light chain.
evidence: This describes the results of chimeric antibody experiments testing individual CDR contributions.

claim: Weak autologous neutralization was observed when mutations surrounding FWRH3-CDRH3 were added to Int6VH.
source: We did observe weak autologous neutralization when mutations surrounding FWRH3-CDRH3 were added to Int6VH.
evidence: This describes the results of a specific chimeric antibody experiment.

claim: Mutations spanning both FWRH1-CDRH1 and FWRH3-CDRH3 of the mature VH together were required to obtain heterologous neutralization.
source: Mutations spanning both FWRH1-CDRH1 and FWRH3-CDRH3 of the mature VH together were required to obtain heterologous neutralization, consistent with the cryo-EM map of key antigen contacts (Figures 3 and 4A).
evidence: This describes the results of chimeric antibody experiments and relates them to structural data.

claim: The determinants of autologous and heterologous neutralization in this antibody lineage were different, in which autologous virus neutralization required less SHM and was facilitated by residues spanning CDRH2-FWRH3-CDRH3.
source: Interestingly, the determinants of autologous and heterologous neutralization in this antibody lineage were different, in which autologous virus neutralization required less SHM and was facilitated by residues spanning CDRH2-FWRH3-CDRH3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes a key finding about the different requirements for autologous versus heterologous neutralization.

claim: Reversion of all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR) resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity.
source: To determine the importance of the framework residues and examine loss of function, we reverted all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR). This reversion resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity, demonstrating that residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization, as has been noted for other HIV bnAbs (Figure 4A,B; Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the results of a reversion experiment and compares to other antibodies, supported by citation.

claim: Residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization.
source: To determine the importance of the framework residues and examine loss of function, we reverted all framework mutations in the mature VH back to the inferred naive BCR residues (∆FWR). This reversion resulted in no detectable binding or neutralization activity, demonstrating that residues in the heavy chain FWRs are essential for QA013.2 binding and neutralization, as has been noted for other HIV bnAbs (Figure 4A,B; Klein et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the reversion experiment.

claim: Reversion of FWRH1 mutations resulted in a 733-fold increase in IC50 for neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3.
source: We also observed a dramatic reduction in heterologous virus neutralization for these same VH chimeric antibodies (∆FWRH1 or ∆CDRH1). Specifically, we observed 733-fold and 250-fold increases in the IC50 for ∆FWRH1 and ∆CDRH1 chimeric antibodies respectively, corresponding to decreased neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1 mutations on heterologous neutralization.

claim: Reversion of FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations resulted in a 250-fold increase in IC50 for neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3.
source: We also observed a dramatic reduction in heterologous virus neutralization for these same VH chimeric antibodies (∆FWRH1 or ∆CDRH1). Specifically, we observed 733-fold and 250-fold increases in the IC50 for ∆FWRH1 and ∆CDRH1 chimeric antibodies respectively, corresponding to decreased neutralization of clade C virus QC406.F3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations on heterologous neutralization.

claim: Reversion of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 led to weakened binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (KD = 40.6 nM) relative to the mature bnAb.
source: Reversion of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 also led to weakened binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer (KD = 40.6 nM) relative to the mature bnAb (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRH1-CDRH1 mutations on binding affinity.

claim: When the CDRH3 was reverted back to naïve (∆CDR3VH), binding and neutralization of both autologous and heterologous virus was maintained, but there was an impact on potency across all viruses tested.
source: When the CDRH3 was reverted back to naïve (∆CDR3VH), binding and neutralization of both autologous and heterologous virus was maintained, but there was an impact on potency across all viruses tested; although this antibody could still neutralize a heterologous clade C variant, it did not neutralize SF162 at the highest antibody concentration tested (Figures 3 and 4A,B).
evidence: This describes the effect of reverting CDRH3 mutations on neutralization.

claim: The CDRH3 does contribute to the overall breadth and potency of QA013.2, while mutations in FWRH1-CDRH1 are critical for achieving complete cross-clade Tier two neutralization breadth.
source: These data suggest that the CDRH3 does contribute to the overall breadth and potency of QA013.2, while mutations in FWRH1-CDRH1 are critical for achieving complete cross-clade Tier two neutralization breadth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimeric antibody experiments.

claim: Four of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 individually contributed to the mature bnAb's ability to neutralize autologous and heterologous virus.
source: We found that four of the six residues spanning FWRH1-CDRH1 individually contributed to the mature bnAb's ability to neutralize autologous and heterologous virus.
evidence: This describes the results of point mutation experiments.

claim: Residues E26, G28, and I24 were most critical, with average increase in IC50 of 191-, 27-, and 25-fold, respectively, across all pseudoviruses tested when these residues were reverted to naïve.
source: Residues E26, G28, and I24 were most critical, with average increase in IC50 of 191-, 27-, and 25-fold, respectively, across all pseudoviruses tested when these residues were reverted to naïve (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This quantifies the contribution of specific residues to neutralization potency.

claim: Reversion of individual CDRH3 residues did not abolish neutralization.
source: While reversion of individual CDRH3 residues did not abolish neutralization, which correlates with the chimeric antibody results (Figure 4), one residue in particular (D106) demonstrated a much higher IC50 value when mutated back to naive.
evidence: This describes the results of point mutation experiments in CDRH3.

claim: D106 is adjacent to the GDIR motif in the structure.
source: D106 is adjacent to the GDIR motif in the structure.
evidence: This describes the structural location of residue D106.

claim: Reversion of D106 to naive did not inhibit clade A autologous virus neutralization, but did substantially impact heterologous neutralization, with an average 40-fold increase in IC50 across all tested pseudoviruses.
source: Reversion of this residue to naive did not inhibit clade A autologous virus neutralization, but did substantially impact heterologous neutralization, with an average 40-fold increase in IC50 across all tested pseudoviruses (Figure 5E).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of the D106V mutation on neutralization.

claim: The D106V point mutant only resulted in a modest decrease in binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer relative to the mature bnAb.
source: However, the D106V point mutant only resulted in a modest decrease in binding to heterologous BG505.SOSIP.664 trimer relative to the mature bnAb (Figure 5F).
evidence: This describes the binding effect of the D106V mutation.

claim: While D106 is not critical for Env binding, this residue does contribute to heterologous neutralization, likely by interacting directly with the linear GDIR motif.
source: These data suggest that while D106 is not critical for Env binding, this residue does contribute to heterologous neutralization, likely by interacting directly with the linear GDIR motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the D106V mutation data.

claim: Although the antibody paratope of QA013.2 includes the CDRH3, where interaction with the N332 glycan and GDIR motif occurs, the QA013.2 paratope is also comprised of critical residues in FWRH1 and CDRH1.
source: Taken together, it is clear that although the antibody paratope of QA013.2 includes the CDRH3, where interaction with the N332 glycan and GDIR motif occurs, the QA013.2 paratope is also comprised of critical residues in FWRH1 and CDRH1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Reversion of residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 abrogated antibody binding to BG505.SOSIP.664 heterologous Env (KD = 1.3 µM) relative to the mature bnAb by more than 400-fold.
source: Reversion of the residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 abrogated antibody binding to BG505.SOSIP.664 heterologous Env (KD = 1.3 µM) relative to the mature bnAb by more than 400-fold.
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRL2-FWRL3 mutations on binding affinity.

claim: Reversion of residues present in FWRL2-FWRL3 resulted in an average 19-fold increase in IC50 (range 6–42 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values.
source: Reversion of residues present in FWRL2-FWRL3 resulted in an average 19-fold increase in IC50 (range 6–42 fold) and reversion of residues in CDRL3 caused a 14-fold increase in average IC50 (range 1–41 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values (Figure 6A).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting FWRL2-FWRL3 mutations on neutralization potency.

claim: Reversion of residues in CDRL3 caused a 14-fold increase in average IC50 (range 1–41 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values.
source: Reversion of residues present in FWRL2-FWRL3 resulted in an average 19-fold increase in IC50 (range 6–42 fold) and reversion of residues in CDRL3 caused a 14-fold increase in average IC50 (range 1–41 fold) across all pseudoviruses tested when compared to the mature bnAb IC50 values (Figure 6A).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of reverting CDRL3 mutations on neutralization potency.

claim: Residues in FWRL2-FWRL3 and CDRL3 contribute to the mature bnAb's binding affinity and neutralization potency, with residues in FWRL2-FWRL3 appearing to have a larger influence on bnAb binding.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that residues in FWRL2-FWRL3 and CDRL3, which are situated along the cleft between heavy and light chains and near the N332 glycan, contribute to the mature bnAb's binding affinity and neutralization potency, with residues in FWRL2-FWRL3 appearing to have a larger influence on bnAb binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the light chain mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 do not interact directly with the N332 glycan on Env.
source: Notably, the residues spanning FWRL2-FWRL3 do not interact directly with the N332 glycan on Env.
evidence: This describes the structural observation about FWRL2-FWRL3 residues.

claim: The residues in FWRL3 may influence the conformation of residues in the adjacent CDRL3 loop, which interacts with the N332 glycan.
source: However, the residues in FWRL3 may influence the conformation of residues in the adjacent CDRL3 loop, which interacts with the N332 glycan.
evidence: This is an inference about the structural role of FWRL3 residues.

claim: The residues in FWRL2 interact with FWRH4 of the Fab heavy chain (residues 117–120) which follows the CDRH3 loop.
source: Furthermore, the residues in FWRL2 interact with FWRH4 of the Fab heavy chain (residues 117–120) which follows the CDRH3 loop (Figure 6C).
evidence: This describes a structural interaction observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Mutational antigenic profiling was used to interrogate the effect of all functionally tolerated single amino acid mutations in BG505.W6.C2 T332N Env on viral escape when under selective pressure from the mature QA013.2 bnAb.
source: We used mutational antigenic profiling to interrogate the effect of all functionally tolerated single amino acid mutations in BG505.W6.C2 T332N Env on viral escape when under selective pressure from the mature QA013.2 bnAb (Dingens et al., 2017; Figure 7).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used for antigenic profiling, with citation.

claim: In addition to mutations that disrupt the N301 and N332 potential N-linked glycosylation sites (PNGS) or alter the GDIR motif, viral escape via mutations in the V1 loop was also observed.
source: In addition to the more traditional signatures of Env escape from V3/glycan-specific bnAbs, including mutations that disrupt the N301 and N332 potential N-linked glycosylation sites (PNGS) or alter the GDIR motif (Dingens et al., 2019), we also observed viral escape via mutations in the V1 loop (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This describes the results of the antigenic profiling experiment, with citation.

claim: Enrichment of viral escape mutations was strongest at sites D325, R327, and H330.
source: In addition to the two PNGS, enrichment of viral escape mutations was strongest at sites D325, R327, and H330; validation of these data using pseudoviruses with individual mutations in TZM-bl neutralization assays showed that mutations to these sites can result in >32-fold change in IC50 relative to the wild-type BG505.T332N (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This describes the results of the antigenic profiling and validation experiments.

claim: Mutations to sites D325, R327, and H330 can result in >32-fold change in IC50 relative to the wild-type BG505.T332N.
source: In addition to the two PNGS, enrichment of viral escape mutations was strongest at sites D325, R327, and H330; validation of these data using pseudoviruses with individual mutations in TZM-bl neutralization assays showed that mutations to these sites can result in >32-fold change in IC50 relative to the wild-type BG505.T332N (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of specific escape mutations on neutralization.

claim: Not all mutations to sites D325, R327, and H330 resulted in viral escape.
source: However, not all mutations to these sites resulted in viral escape.
evidence: This notes that escape is mutation-specific, not just site-specific.

claim: While D325E was enriched in mutational antigenic profiling and had a >32-fold effect in the TZM-bl assay, D325N/S mutants were not enriched and had negligible effects when tested individually via TZM-bl neutralization assay.
source: Similar to 10–1074 (Dingens et al., 2019), while D325E was enriched in mutational antigenic profiling and had a >32-fold effect in the TZM-bl assay, D325N/S mutants were not enriched and had negligible effects when tested individually via TZM-bl neutralization assay.
evidence: This describes mutation-specific effects and compares to another antibody, with citation.

claim: Viral escape in the V1 loop occurred at two sites that are adjacent in the BG505 structure; D141 and R151 (HXB2 numbering), both of which caused a modest ~3-fold change in IC50 relative to the wildtype virus.
source: Viral escape in the V1 loop occurred at two sites that are adjacent in the BG505 structure; D141 and R151 (HXB2 numbering), both of which caused a modest ~3-fold change in IC50 relative to the wildtype virus (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This describes escape mutations in V1 and quantifies their effect.

claim: While the V1 loop of Env does not appear to be in direct contact with QA013.2 Fab in the complex structure, the backbone Cα atoms of the Fab CDRH3 loop and Env V1 loop are within 8 Å of each other.
source: While the V1 loop of Env does not appear to be in direct contact with QA013.2 Fab in the complex structure, the backbone Cα atoms of the Fab CDRH3 loop and Env V1 loop are within 8 Å of each other (Figure 7D), suggesting there could be amino acid side-chain interactions between the two loops that can affect neutralization.
evidence: This describes the structural relationship between V1 and the antibody, and infers potential interactions.

claim: While the glycan at N332 is essential for bnAb neutralization and disrupting this motif results in viral escape, it is not required to achieve antibody binding.
source: Interestingly, while the glycan at N332 is essential for bnAb neutralization and disrupting this motif results in viral escape, we observed that it is not required to achieve antibody binding – as demonstrated by the mature bnAb binding to the gp120s from the autologous clade D and BG505.W6.C1 viruses, both of which lack the PNGS at site 332 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a distinction between binding and neutralization requirements.

claim: The mature bnAb binds to gp120s from the autologous clade D and BG505.W6.C1 viruses, both of which lack the PNGS at site 332.
source: Interestingly, while the glycan at N332 is essential for bnAb neutralization and disrupting this motif results in viral escape, we observed that it is not required to achieve antibody binding – as demonstrated by the mature bnAb binding to the gp120s from the autologous clade D and BG505.W6.C1 viruses, both of which lack the PNGS at site 332 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes binding data for viruses lacking the N332 glycan.

claim: The binding to viruses lacking N332 glycan, while measurable, is too weak to confer neutralization.
source: It is likely that this binding, while measurable, is too weak to confer neutralization, confirming the importance of the N332 glycan.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the N332 glycan based on binding and neutralization data.

claim: QA013.2 bnAb has previously been shown to potently neutralize tier two viruses from clades A, B, and C, as well as several tier three viruses from clades B and C, but it did not neutralize clade D or A/D recombinant viruses.
source: The QA013.2 bnAb has previously been shown to potently neutralize tier two viruses from clades A, B, and C, as well as several tier three viruses from clades B and C, but it did not neutralize clade D or A/D recombinant viruses (Williams et al., 2018).
evidence: This summarizes previous findings about the neutralization breadth of QA013.2, with citation.

claim: Elimination of the glycan at N301 abolished all neutralization activity despite the presence of the N332 glycan in BG505.W6.C2 T332N.
source: To confirm the dependence of QA013.2 bnAb on the glycan at N301, we generated a N to K mutation at position 301 in BG505.W6.C2 T332N, which is the virus used for antigenic profiling, as K301 was identified as a major escape mutation (Figure 7). Elimination of the glycan at N301 abolished all neutralization activity despite the presence of the N332 glycan in BG505.W6.C2 T332N (Figure 8).
evidence: This describes the result of a specific mutation experiment testing the role of N301.

claim: Both N301 and N332 glycans in combination are required to achieve bnAb neutralization.
source: These data demonstrate that both N301 and N332 glycans in combination are required to achieve bnAb neutralization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the N301K mutation experiment.

claim: QA013.2 neutralized clade A but not clade D viruses.
source: Similar to the findings with autologous virus, QA013.2 neutralized clade A but not clade D viruses; interestingly, the bnAb also did not neutralize D/A recombinant variants.
evidence: This describes the clade-specific neutralization pattern of QA013.2.

claim: The bnAb also did not neutralize D/A recombinant variants.
source: Similar to the findings with autologous virus, QA013.2 neutralized clade A but not clade D viruses; interestingly, the bnAb also did not neutralize D/A recombinant variants.
evidence: This describes the neutralization pattern for recombinant viruses.

claim: Clade A virus neutralization was not universal, notably those viruses missing either glycan or the GDIR motif were not neutralized.
source: Clade A virus neutralization was not universal, notably those viruses missing either glycan or the GDIR motif were not neutralized, which aligns with the predictions of key antigen contacts identified in the cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 bound to native-like Env trimer (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the epitope requirements for neutralization based on testing multiple viruses.

claim: The mature bnAb is only capable of neutralizing viruses that contain N301, N332, and the linear GDIR motif.
source: The mature bnAb is only capable of neutralizing viruses that contain N301, N332, and the linear GDIR motif (Figure 8).
evidence: This summarizes the epitope requirements for neutralization.

claim: All viruses that are neutralized by QA013.2 contain a (negative charge/branched hydrophobic/positive charge) motif in the final 10 residues of the V1 loop, except MK184.W0.D1.
source: Indeed, we noted that all viruses that are neutralized by QA013.2 contain a (negative charge/branched hydrophobic/positive charge) motif in the final 10 residues of the V1 loop, except MK184.W0.D1, which is a clade C/D recombinant with clade D V1-V5 sequence (Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in neutralized viruses, with citation for virus characterization.

claim: The four viruses that contained the main antigenic contacts in Env (N301, N332, and GDIR) but were not neutralized by the mature bnAb were either subtype D in variable loops 1 and 2 (D/A recombinants) or they lacked the [negative charge/branched hydrophobic/positive charge] motif in V1.
source: The four viruses that contained the main antigenic contacts in Env (N301, N332, and GDIR) but were not neutralized by the mature bnAb were either subtype D in variable loops 1 and 2 (D/A recombinants; Wu et al., 2006), or they lacked this [negative charge/branched hydrophobic/positive charge] in V1.
evidence: This describes viruses that have the core epitope but are not neutralized, with citation.

claim: The mature bnAb can only neutralize viruses from clades A, B, and C, not clade D.
source: Overall, the neutralization results from this expanded panel demonstrates that the mature bnAb can only neutralize viruses from clades A, B, and C, not clade D (Figure 8), as suggested by studies using a smaller virus panel (Williams et al., 2018) and that V1 influences the antibody's function.
evidence: This summarizes the clade-specific neutralization breadth, with citation to previous work.

claim: V1 influences the antibody's function.
source: Overall, the neutralization results from this expanded panel demonstrates that the mature bnAb can only neutralize viruses from clades A, B, and C, not clade D (Figure 8), as suggested by studies using a smaller virus panel (Williams et al., 2018) and that V1 influences the antibody's function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neutralization data and V1 motif analysis.

claim: HIV superinfection elicits bnAbs more frequently than single infection.
source: HIV superinfection elicits bnAbs more frequently than single infection, providing clues of how to elicit such responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background/motivation for the study.

claim: BnAb QA013.2 bound initial and superinfecting viral Env, despite its probable naive progenitor only recognizing the superinfecting strain.
source: BnAb QA013.2 bound initial and superinfecting viral Env, despite its probable naive progenitor only recognizing the superinfecting strain, suggesting both viruses influenced this lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Both viruses influenced the QA013.2 lineage.
source: BnAb QA013.2 bound initial and superinfecting viral Env, despite its probable naive progenitor only recognizing the superinfecting strain, suggesting both viruses influenced this lineage.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the abstract based on the binding data.

claim: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 bound to native-like trimer showed recognition of V3 signatures (N301/N332 and GDIR).
source: A 4.15 Å cryo-EM structure of QA013.2 bound to native-like trimer showed recognition of V3 signatures (N301/N332 and GDIR).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: QA013.2 relies less on CDRH3 and more on framework and CDRH1 for affinity and breadth compared to other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs.
source: QA013.2 relies less on CDRH3 and more on framework and CDRH1 for affinity and breadth compared to other V3/glycan-specific bnAbs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Viral escape was achieved by changes in the structurally-defined epitope and by mutations in V1.
source: Antigenic profiling revealed that viral escape was achieved by changes in the structurally-defined epitope and by mutations in V1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Developing a vaccine that elicits broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against HIV is considered critical to achieving protection from the extensive diversity of circulating HIV subtypes.
source: Developing a vaccine that elicits broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) against HIV is considered critical to achieving protection from the extensive diversity of circulating HIV subtypes (Burton and Hangartner, 2016; Doria-Rose, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement of scientific consensus supported by citations.

claim: The potency and protective efficacy of bnAbs has been demonstrated in passive immunization trials.
source: The potency and protective efficacy of these bnAbs has been demonstrated in passive immunization trials (Pegu et al., 2017), however thus far, no vaccine design has been capable of eliciting potent HIV bnAbs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to passive immunization trials.

claim: No vaccine design has been capable of eliciting potent HIV bnAbs.
source: The potency and protective efficacy of these bnAbs has been demonstrated in passive immunization trials (Pegu et al., 2017), however thus far, no vaccine design has been capable of eliciting potent HIV bnAbs.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of HIV vaccine development.

claim: HIV-specific bnAbs typically take years to develop in adults, requiring exposure of the immune system to significant, evolving viral diversity.
source: In part, this may be because HIV-specific bnAbs typically take years to develop in adults, requiring exposure of the immune system to significant, evolving viral diversity, and have unusual features including extended complementarity determining regions (CDRs), widespread somatic hypermutation (SHM), and polyreactivity (Mascola and Haynes, 2013).
evidence: This describes characteristics of bnAb development, supported by citation.

claim: HIV-specific bnAbs have unusual features including extended complementarity determining regions (CDRs), widespread somatic hypermutation (SHM), and polyreactivity.
source: In part, this may be because HIV-specific bnAbs typically take years to develop in adults, requiring exposure of the immune system to significant, evolving viral diversity, and have unusual features including extended complementarity determining regions (CDRs), widespread somatic hypermutation (SHM), and polyreactivity (Mascola and Haynes, 2013).
evidence: This describes characteristics of bnAbs, supported by citation.

claim: Plasma from SI individuals is more broad and potently neutralizing than plasma obtained from time-matched samples of single HIV infection.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that plasma from SI individuals is more broad and potently neutralizing than plasma obtained from time-matched samples of single HIV infection (Cortez et al., 2012; Powell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: QA013.2 uses unique gene segments (VH3-7*01 VD1-1*01 VJ5*02 and VL1-40*01 VJ2*01).
source: QA013.2 uses unique gene segments (VH3-7*01 VD1-1*01 VJ5*02 and VL1-40*01 VJ2*01), has moderate levels of somatic hypermutation (≤ 20%), and unlike many HIV bnAbs, was not found to be polyreactive (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the genetic characteristics of QA013.2.

claim: QA013.2 has moderate levels of somatic hypermutation (≤ 20%).
source: QA013.2 uses unique gene segments (VH3-7*01 VD1-1*01 VJ5*02 and VL1-40*01 VJ2*01), has moderate levels of somatic hypermutation (≤ 20%), and unlike many HIV bnAbs, was not found to be polyreactive (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This quantifies the level of SHM in QA013.2.

claim: Unlike many HIV bnAbs, QA013.2 was not found to be polyreactive.
source: QA013.2 uses unique gene segments (VH3-7*01 VD1-1*01 VJ5*02 and VL1-40*01 VJ2*01), has moderate levels of somatic hypermutation (≤ 20%), and unlike many HIV bnAbs, was not found to be polyreactive (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a functional property of QA013.2, with reference to a figure showing polyreactivity testing.
